Fake Online Pharmacy UK Scams: How to Spot and Avoid Illegal Medicine Sites

Thousands of fake online pharmacies operate across the internet, selling fake medicines that could seriously harm your health or cost you money.

Published 2026-05-15 · Beat the Scam Editorial Team · 6 min read

fake online pharmacy UKillegal online pharmacy scamcounterfeit medicine UKverify legitimate online pharmacyNHS registered pharmacy check
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.
On this page
  1. What is this scam?
  2. Warning signs to look for

What is this scam?

Fake online pharmacies are websites that appear to sell legitimate prescription and over-the-counter medicines but are actually run by criminals. They may sell counterfeit pills that contain no active ingredient, wrong doses, or dangerous fillers—or nothing at all. Some sites steal your payment and personal data without sending anything. Others sell genuinely dangerous substances that mimic prescription medicines but contain harmful chemicals. The UK has thousands of illegal pharmacy sites, many based overseas but targeting British customers. They advertise heavily on search engines and social media, often at suspiciously low prices. Unlike registered UK pharmacies regulated by the General Pharmaceutical Council, these operations have no oversight and no accountability if something goes wrong.

Warning signs to look for

  • No visible pharmacy registration number or it doesn't match when you check on the General Pharmaceutical Council website.
  • Prices far below what legitimate UK pharmacies charge—especially for prescription-only medicines like antibiotics or blood pressure tablets.
  • No requirement for a valid prescription, or they accept dodgy online 'consultations' lasting seconds from unlicensed practitioners.
  • Poor grammar and spelling on the website, inconsistent branding, or a cheap-looking design.
  • No UK address listed, only a PO Box, or an address that doesn't match a real pharmacy location.
  • Payment only by untraceable methods like cryptocurrency, gift cards, or Western Union instead of standard card or bank transfer.
  • No live customer service phone number or email support, or responses from generic addresses like 'support@pharmacy.co.uk'.
  • Claims to sell medicines without expiry dates listed, or pills in unmarked or badly printed packaging.

How this scam works step by step

The scam typically begins when you search for a medicine online or click an ad on social media. The fake pharmacy site looks professional—it has logos, terms and conditions, and customer reviews (often fake). You add items to your basket and are asked for personal details: your name, address, email, and payment information. Some sites ask for a photo of a prescription; others skip this entirely or accept obviously forged ones. You pay by card or bank transfer. At this point, several outcomes are possible. The scammer simply takes your money and you receive nothing, only silence or generic 'your order is processing' emails. Alternatively, the site sends counterfeit or unlicensed tablets in generic packaging with no product information. If you use these, you may experience dangerous side effects because you don't know what's actually inside them. Meanwhile, your payment details and personal information have been captured for identity theft or sold to other criminals. Your bank may not refund you because you made a voluntary transaction.

How to verify if it is genuine

Always check the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC) online pharmacy checker at gphc.org.uk before buying. Type the pharmacy's name and you'll see if it's registered. Legitimate UK online pharmacies display their GPhC registration number prominently. Call the pharmacy's phone number (not one on their site—look it up separately) and ask about your prescription. Ask which NHS trust they're affiliated with or which medical wholesaler supplies them. Check the NHS or your GP's practice website for their recommendation—GPs often have links to safe online dispensaries. Look for https (secure) in the web address and a padlock icon. Verify the address matches on Google Maps. Ask a pharmacist: if you're unsure, ring your local high street pharmacy and ask if they recognise the site. For further guidance on spotting fake websites in general, see our guide on /guides/is-this-website-a-scam/. Registered UK pharmacies will happily verify themselves because they have nothing to hide.

What to do if you have already interacted

Stop using any medicine you received immediately—do not take it. If you believe it's counterfeit, contact your GP or NHS 111 and explain what you took and where it came from; they can assess any health risk. Report the site to the NCSC's Suspicious Email Reporting Service if you received phishing emails from them. Contact Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or report online at actionfraud.police.uk with the site URL, date, amount paid, and any confirmations you received. If you paid by card, contact your bank's fraud team at once—they may stop the transaction or reverse it within 120 days. If you paid by bank transfer, alert your bank immediately; recovery is harder but sometimes possible if money hasn't been withdrawn. Keep all emails, receipts, and screenshots. Change your passwords for email and any accounts you used on the site. Monitor your credit file at Clearscore or Experian for suspicious activity. Do not respond to any follow-up emails from the site, and do not order again.

Reporting this scam in the UK

Report fake online pharmacies to Action Fraud—the national fraud reporting service—by calling 0300 123 2040 (Monday to Friday, 8am–8pm) or reporting online at actionfraud.police.uk. They log the report and pass it to local police and Trading Standards. Contact the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk if you received phishing emails directing you to the fake site. Citizens Advice consumer helpline (0808 223 1133) can advise you on refunds if you paid by card. Report the pharmacy to the General Pharmaceutical Council at gphc.org.uk to have the fake operation flagged for enforcement. If the medicines endangered your health, also report to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) at mhra.gov.uk. Forward any SMS or text scams advertising illegal pharmacies to 7726 (Spam). Provide as much detail as possible: the full website URL, the pharmacy name it claimed, dates of purchase, and any screenshots. These reports help authorities shut down fake sites and warn other consumers.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if an online pharmacy is actually registered and legitimate in the UK?

Use the General Pharmaceutical Council (GPhC) online pharmacy checker at gphc.org.uk—it's the only official list. Type in the pharmacy name and you'll see if it's registered, which NHS trust oversees it, and its official address. Never rely on what the website says about itself. Call the pharmacy directly on a number you find independently (not from their site) and ask them to confirm their GPhC number.

I already paid money to a fake pharmacy and received nothing. Can I get my money back?

If you paid by card, contact your bank's fraud team immediately—they may authorise a 'chargeback' within 120 days. If you paid by bank transfer, call your bank straight away; recovery is less certain but they may be able to freeze the receiving account. Report the site to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and keep all evidence. Don't expect a full refund, but banks sometimes recover funds if they act quickly.

What should I do if I've already taken medicine from a fake pharmacy and I'm worried about my health?

Contact NHS 111 immediately or visit your GP and tell them exactly what you took, when, and where it came from. They can assess any health risk and advise on treatment. Do not take any more of the medicine. If you experience severe symptoms like chest pain or difficulty breathing, call 999. Your GP may want to run tests depending on what the counterfeit was supposed to be.

What's the best way to report a fake online pharmacy?

Report to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040 or actionfraud.police.uk) with the website URL and date you used it. Also report the pharmacy to the General Pharmaceutical Council at gphc.org.uk so they can flag it for enforcement action. If you received scam emails, forward them to the NCSC at report@phishing.gov.uk. Report SMS scams to 7726. The more reports, the faster authorities can shut sites down.

Fast checks

  • Pause before sending money or credentials
  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
